stories.headline: Microsoft benchmark finds agents often claim success but leave databases wrong
stories.standfirst: Microsoft's ThinkingBox checks what an AI agent actually changed in a database, not what it said. Across 121,680 trials, the authors say 67% of failures were clean tool calls with wrong values.
body: Microsoft's Copilot Studio team and the data company Toloka published ThinkingBox on 3 October, a benchmark that scores AI agents on the state they leave in a database rather than on their replies. The authors say that across 121,680 trials, 67.24 per cent of failures still called tools cleanly but wrote wrong field values. No outside group has reproduced the numbers.

The write-up, posted on Hugging Face, runs 18 models against 507 business-workflow tasks inside isolated tool sessions. Each task is attempted 20 times, because the authors argue that one success is not reliability. Their stated thesis is that a tool call is not an outcome. Collaborators include researchers at the University of Pittsburgh and Northwestern University.

On a single attempt, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 leads at 67.16 per cent, the authors report. Moonshot's Kimi-K3 solves 93.89 per cent of tasks at least once but only 13.41 per cent every time. Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 each pass 241 tasks on all 20 tries, the most consistent results in the table.

The authors also price dependability. They say GPT-5.4 has the lowest cost per dependable task at $6.80, while GPT-6 Astra reaches more consistent results, 231 tasks, at $7.45 a task. Roughly four in five failures come from tool handling rather than reasoning, according to the write-up, which suggests the weak point is plumbing, not intelligence.

The framework is MIT-licensed and the benchmark data uses the CDLA-Permissive-2.0 licence. Both are on Hugging Face as microsoft/ThinkingBox-Bench and as an OpenEnv environment under BSD-3-Clause. Because the results come from the benchmark's own authors, and model makers have not commented, the rankings should be read as one team's measurement until others rerun them.

stories.headline: Meta opens Muse Gadgets, a DIY kit for building AI hardware
stories.standfirst: Meta says its Apache 2.0 kit pairs ESP32 firmware and a Linux SDK with its Muse agent, and 5,000 USB-C Home Link devices are due within weeks.
body: Meta has announced Muse Gadgets, an open-source project that lets hobbyists build their own AI hardware, The Decoder reported on 3 October. It includes firmware for ESP32 boards and a Linux SDK for connecting homemade devices to Muse, Meta's AI agent. The code is Apache 2.0 licensed, and the project has a Discord community.

Meta also built a device of its own. The Muse Home Link is a small USB-C gadget that connects Muse to a home network, letting it control any device with an HTTPS interface, such as a TV or speaker, according to Meta. The company says 5,000 units have been produced and should ship within weeks, free for Muse subscribers while supplies last.

The project is also listed on Product Hunt, which describes it as Meta's open-source kit for building your own AI gadgets. We found no independent builds or tests of the firmware or the SDK, so what they can do rests on Meta's description. The Decoder suggests Meta may use the project to learn which form factors people actually want, a reading the company has not stated.

Muse itself has become a hit with consumers, Wired reported on 3 October, with millions downloading the assistant and connecting it to bank accounts, messages or health data. Researchers have since extracted its internal instructions, which Meta told Wired it meant to make accessible in the interest of transparency. The Gadgets kit would extend that agent from the phone into the home.

stories.headline: White House names Clayton to lead AI 'Super Intelligence Force'
stories.standfirst: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead a White House task force with 120 days to report on AI's risks and opportunities, the Wall Street Journal reported.
body: The White House has created a task force to examine AI's risks and opportunities, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday. It is to recommend what role the federal government should play in overseeing the technology, with a report due within 120 days. Reuters relayed the account, which cites the task force's head, Jay Clayton.

The group is known as the "Super Intelligence Force", and Clayton, who heads the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, told the Journal he would lead it. He would effectively serve as President Donald Trump's AI czar, according to Reuters. The report also cites a senior White House official. Bloomberg carried the story the same day, attributing it to the Journal.

The appointment follows earlier reporting. CBS News said on Thursday, citing sources, that Clayton was likely to be Trump's pick for AI czar while staying director of national intelligence. The commentator Andrew Curran wrote on X late Saturday that the task force had been renamed the SI Force, citing the Journal.

The Reuters account does not say who else sits on the task force, what budget or legal authority it has, or whether its report would bind agencies. We opened Reuters' version, not the Journal's paywalled article, and found no White House statement confirming the name. The 120-day clock would run into early next year if it started now.

stories.headline: Willison says coding agents mean pay-per-use services need hard spending caps
stories.standfirst: Simon Willison argues cloud services should cut off at a set bill by default, since agents make surprise bills of thousands of dollars easier. AWS and Google Cloud only just added caps.
body: Developer Simon Willison argued on 3 October that pay-by-usage services and APIs should ship with default hard budget caps, a setting that stops service and returns errors once a monthly limit is reached. His post says soft caps that only send warning emails fail, because people sleep through them while bills grow.

Willison ties the proposal to coding agents. In his telling, they make it easier to deploy applications that can generate large, unexpected charges. He puts the typical damage at several hundred or several thousand dollars, with surprise bills above $10,000 the point where it becomes serious, and says some developers avoid AWS for personal projects out of fear of exactly that.

He credits two providers with moving. AWS launched spending limits on 16 September, he writes: when usage reaches the cap, the project pauses for the month, though he says the feature is limited to select customers. Google Cloud added Spend Caps in July, letting users cap spending on specific services inside a project.

Willison proposes that turning a cap off should need explicit wording: "Remove the budget cap. My application will not be shut down if I exceed the configured budget limit, and I will be responsible for subsequent charges." The post is opinion, not a vendor announcement. Neither AWS nor Google has commented, as far as the sources show.

The argument may matter most to people running agents unattended. A hard cap could turn a runaway loop into an error message instead of an invoice, but it also takes the service down, which is why Willison says it should be the default. He does not say which other providers lack such limits.
